title: Hope for a Tree, Not a Man
overview: Still answering his friends, Job turns to God and grieves how short and fragile human life is, briefly longing for hope beyond death before sinking back into sorrow.

parts.label: Short lives, harsh scrutiny (vv. 1-6)
parts.note: Job says people bloom and fade like flowers and pass like shadows, so why does God watch them so closely and put them on trial? Since no one is flawless and our days are already numbered, he asks God to look away and let him rest, like a hired worker waiting for his day's work to end.

parts.label: A tree can sprout again (vv. 7-12)
parts.note: A cut tree can send up new shoots when its old stump catches the scent of water. A person who dies is like a dried-up lake, and in Job's view he does not rise again for as long as the sky lasts.

parts.label: A wish to be remembered (vv. 13-17)
parts.note: Job wishes God would hide him in the grave until God's anger passed, then call him back, longing for the creature he made, with Job's wrongs sealed away like money in a tied purse. When Job asks whether someone who dies can live again, it sounds more like longing than settled belief, though Christians later read it as reaching toward resurrection.

parts.label: Hope worn away (vv. 18-22)
parts.note: Just as water slowly wears down mountains and stones, Job feels God wearing away human hope until a person dies. As he pictures it, the dead cannot even know whether their children do well or badly, and are left only with their own pain.

disagreement: Christians differ on whether Job here holds a real, if faint, hope of life after death or is only voicing a wish he then lets go of as impossible.
think: When you think about how short life is, does it make your days feel more precious, more unfair, or something else entirely?
